title: Air India Phuket-Delhi Plunge May Have Been Caused by Fly-By-Wire Fault, Not Turbulence
excerpt: India's aviation regulator is investigating a suspected transient technical fault in the A320neo's fly-by-wire system as the leading explanation for the 300-foot altitude drop that injured 17 people.
body:
• India's DGCA is treating a "suspected transient technical fault" in the fly-by-wire system — not turbulence — as the leading hypothesis for the 300-foot altitude drop on Air India flight AI2379
  • Flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been seized, and Airbus has been brought into the investigation from the outset
  • Passenger accounts describe mechanical rumbling sounds inconsistent with clear-air turbulence, pointing toward a possible flight control system anomaly
  • The incident marks Air India's third significant altitude-related event in 14 months, intensifying regulatory scrutiny of the Tata-owned carrier

The sudden 300-foot plunge that injured 17 people aboard Air India flight AI2379 on August 4 may not have been caused by turbulence at all. India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation is now investigating a "suspected transient technical fault" in the Airbus A320neo's fly-by-wire system as its leading hypothesis — a significant departure from Air India's initial characterisation of the event as a "brief in-flight turbulence-related event," according to a DGCA official cited by Outlook India.

What Investigators Are Looking At

The DGCA has secured the aircraft's flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder for examination. Airbus has been brought into the investigation from the outset — a step regulators typically reserve for cases where the aircraft's systems, rather than weather, are under scrutiny.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Zy33OHpLXIU

The A320neo uses a fly-by-wire system in which the pilot's sidestick sends electrical signals to flight computers — Elevator and Aileron Computers (ELACs) and Spoiler and Elevator Computers (SECs) — which then command the actual control surfaces. There is no direct physical connection between the pilot and the flight surfaces. If a corrupted data packet reaches one of these computers, it could command a surface movement that neither pilot intended.

"A loud rumbling noise and shaking/vibrating — almost like the sensation you get during takeoff or landing."

— Passenger account of the moments before the drop, cited by Tech Times

That passenger description is significant because standard clear-air turbulence does not produce takeoff-like mechanical sounds. Aviation safety analysts note that flight control system anomalies, however, can. The distinction between turbulence and a fly-by-wire fault requires entirely different investigations and carries different implications for the airline and for Airbus.

A Pattern That Concerns Regulators

The AI2379 incident arrives during the most sustained period of regulatory pressure Air India has faced since its privatisation by the Tata Group. In June 2025, Air India flight AI171 — a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner — crashed roughly 32 seconds after takeoff from Ahmedabad, killing 241 of the 242 people aboard and 19 on the ground. That investigation remains ongoing, with the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau examining a fuel cutoff as a central finding.

Just 38 hours after the AI171 crash, a separate Air India flight — AI-187 from Delhi to Vienna — dropped nearly 900 feet after takeoff, triggering stall warnings and repeated "Don't sink" ground proximity alerts. Both pilots were grounded, and the DGCA summoned Air India's Head of Safety. A subsequent DGCA safety audit flagged recurring maintenance deficiencies across Air India's fleet.

AI2379 now represents the carrier's third significant altitude-related incident in 14 months.

The Incident in Detail

Flight AI2379 departed Phuket International Airport at approximately 8:25 AM local time on August 4, carrying 137 passengers — including three infants — and eight crew members. The seven-year-old A320neo (registration VT-EXO) was cruising above 36,000 feet near the eastern Indian state of Odisha when it underwent what regulators describe as a "momentary altitude variation" of approximately 300 feet.

The seatbelt sign was off at the time. Thirteen passengers and four of the six cabin crew were injured. Overhead bins cracked open and ceiling panels fractured as passengers were thrown upward. One flight attendant sustained a severe injury, according to the DGCA. The aircraft recovered and continued to Delhi, landing safely at Indira Gandhi International Airport.

As of August 5, all 13 injured passengers had been discharged. Four crew members continued to receive medical treatment. India's Union Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu visited injured passengers at Fortis Hospital in Vasant Kunj on August 5.

A320neo Fly-By-Wire Systems Have Flagged Before

The fly-by-wire hypothesis is not without precedent on the A320 platform. In November 2025, Airbus identified that intense solar radiation could corrupt data critical to the flight controls of A320-family aircraft, triggering a worldwide software patch. The DGCA ordered an immediate halt to affected flights until the fix was installed, impacting approximately 6,000 jets globally. Air India completed the patch on its affected aircraft.

Whether AI2379's event represents a residual vulnerability from that issue, a different transient fault, or ultimately a weather explanation is what investigators will determine from the black box data. The FDR findings are expected in a preliminary report later in 2026.

What Travelers Should Know

The DGCA has not issued a grounding order or airworthiness directive for A320neo aircraft following this incident. Aviation experts stress that the most effective protection against unexpected cabin events — whether from turbulence or a system fault — remains keeping seatbelts fastened whenever seated, particularly during cruise when the sign is off. The injury distribution on AI2379 underscores this: four of six flight attendants, who cannot remain seated during service, were among the injured.
nri_angle: The investigation raises safety questions for Indian travelers, particularly diaspora members who frequently fly Air India on routes connecting India to Southeast Asia and beyond.
